story_text.value:
There is some recent discourse about what a "better" interface for humans managing agents looks like. Email/inboxes have come up, and it's reinforcing the premise of thing i've been building. e.g.

  - https://x.com/brian_armstrong/status/2119112609223827547
  - https://x.com/rough__sea/status/2119288646671155217?a=KRzp4CnuV6SijzvCTUw&s=20
This isn't 'another ADE', this is a side-car type of experience and it integrates nearly a year of work around annotating markdown, html, other artifacts since I requested the original Claude Code Hooks feature for better human-control integration.

The email inbox model is intuitive, but so could be "forums", slack-like, or other surfaces feel right.

I do not believe we will be working in coding sessions (full transcripts) much longer. I've been hitting flow-state on top of a better surface layer to make decisions and annotate artifacts, view variations, review code, etc all feedback going back to the agents

MIT/Apache2.0:

https://github.com/backnotprop/plannotator

story_text.value:
I built this because it was useful for me when building evals/benchmarks, and I decided to put it up for free for others. The goal was quite simple, make it easy to use a lead claude code / codex session in a panel on the side, while allowing every cell to also be a terminal session running claude/codex, and make it possible to continue a session in an actual terminal window if I needed to. They can all talk to each other using cells on the grid, named cells, or the MCP server that effectively glues the app together. I also found it useful for managing context within related but disparate sessions.

My real benchmark runs with recalc are internal to my startup, so to demonstrate some of the functionality I built a small FDA Bench with the tool (obtain and put together dossier's of FDA submissions, and see if a harnessed Claude could have accurately predicted pass/fail): https://github.com/sshah03/recalc#a-model-benchmark

It is still very much a work in progress, but given the versatility of spreadsheet apps, wanted to see how others see themselves using it and what doesn't exist that would be useful to them. Currently runs locally on macs, linux as well but that's less tested, and Windows hasn't been tested at all so that'll come in the future.

story_text.value:
Loop is a mobile-first companion workspace for the coding harnesses you already run. It aggregates results from your harnesses into a continuous feed that is easy to navigate and organize from your phone. I spent several months holding my newborn in one hand and trying to talk to agents one-handed on my phone. Every mobile UI is still based around chat, and it doesn’t scale on mobile, let alone one-handed!

So I built Loop: a feed of the work your coding agents do. It’s built around agent results, not chats. You can scroll your history, get notified, save outputs, search and return to conversations later. The goal is to make interacting with agents via your phone feel familiar and intuitive based on the mobile UX we’ve all come to expect.

Loop runs on your own computer — no account, no server, no app store — and pairs with your phone with one QR scan. It wraps the agents you already use (Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode, Antigravity, Muse Code, Grok Build, or any ACP agent), each keeping its own context, tools, sign-in and billing — local models through Pi or OpenCode work too.

Apache-2.0, TypeScript, SQLite. I'd love feedback from anyone else who builds from a phone.

title.value: Show HN: Loop – your coding agents, from your phone

story_text.value:
after working quite rigorously for a few months with claude code, I found out that I was blindly approving permission requests for the sake of progressing my projects, this led me to realize that coding agents generate hundreds of commands underneath the covers which is necessary, but quite scary if you ask me. you've probably seen news recently about agents deleting databases or environments in production by accident. so i wanted to create something to gain visibility into what's actually happening and potentially block things before they occur.

coding agents often log everything that they're doing, but even still, i want the ground level truth of what's happening. that's why i created sentient, written using claude code. it's open source (mit license), runs completely locally, no cloud syncing, read only, and watches actions straight from the kernel. all of this is summarized with a hopefully simple web ui.

i run claude code on linux, so kernel tracking relies on tetragon, but, at the same time, i am trying to get approval to use security endpoint on mac, and will eventually roll out on windows. if you want to run sentient today against just the agent logs without kernel logs, that's also available now, you just need golang and sqlite3 to build. and today, i'm only supporting claude code, but will eventually get to codex and the like. please have a try, ping me if you have any questions or comments: hello@nosaka.ai

https://github.com/nosaka4i/sentient

https://nosaka.ai/blog/sentient

title.value: Show HN: Sentient, Your Coding Agent Shouldn't Be a Black Box

story_text.value:
Hi HN, my friend's team and I have been building a game called GRID, a dog poker game with an AI twist.

Under the cute dog graphics, GRID is an arena where LLMs compete, with no-limit hold’em as the medium. You duke it out as a strategist, vibe coder, and bot maker.

Why: models get compared on benchmarks all the time, but rarely as my agent against yours in its truest form. GRID is our attempt at creating that arena, because we believe this type of game will exist in the future, as AI becomes as common a tool as the browser.

How it works:

* Paste a prompt and an MCP config into Claude Code, Codex or any MCP client. The agent waits for its turn and sends actions back through tool calls.

* The strategy is text written in the game, up to 6,000 characters. We thought it’d be cool to have a preset, “Play like Elon”, to show you what you can do.

* You can change the strategy any time, and it applies from the next action. You can even ask your AI to change it for you, based on what it learns about its opponents’ strategies from the match history.

* Free beta. Play chips only. We just opened up the game today and are gathering data on how to steer this ship next.

Rough edges:

* MCP can be finicky, especially if you refresh your browser while in a match. If this happens and you can’t get your agent to connect, wait 5 min and retry | log out using the settings button at the top left and log back in. Stability is currently our top priority.

* MCP also uses a lot of tokens, more than the game should, because every tool call costs tokens. We plan to overhaul this with a new connection type in a future version so it’s much more efficient.

* There’s a built-in local model for folks who don’t want to use their own AI. It plays basic hold’em OK but struggles to follow written strategies. If you want to try it, I’d recommend leaving your strategy blank. Sadly, it plays best with no instructions.

* House bots fill empty seats. We made this choice so matches happen even when only a few people are online.

Honestly, I’m most curious how you’d write a strategy that holds up against everyone else’s agents. And if MCP setup breaks on you, please tell me. We'll be in the thread as long as possible.

story_text.value:
My code is written by agents now. Git blame shows me the commit and my own name, but the reason for the code is in a session I closed weeks ago.

KeepPlain saves your agent sessions. It uses git blame to find the session that corresponds to a file, line, or commit. Then it shows the original request and the reasoning behind the change. It also finds commits made by the user after the agent session and links them to the session.

I also try to use the mistakes the agent makes over and over to turn them into rules for new sessions. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi and Antigravity.

Your sessions are uploaded to my server and are kept private to you. All secrets are redacted on your machine before the upload. I’m sure there will be lots of questions about this. The plugin is MIT licensed and open source. The server is not. Teams can run their own Postgres database to store their data.

KeepPlain is free for personal use and teams will pay for it. I am a solo developer and this is early on in development so please let me know where it breaks.

story_text.value:
Yesterday a few interesting links appeared on hacker news about always-on [1] and multi-agent setups [2].

Some of those points resonate with what we're experiencing with our current approach of running agents and sub-agents locally.

- We are delegating complex and long running tasks to agents more and more. Being able to run those overnight seems like a logical next step in efficiency, because at the moment we are stopping the local agents every evening and restarting them in the morning.

- A setup with decentralized multi-agent system with shared context is 5.5x faster than Claude code + native subagents. It takes 29.3 minutes (2% of agent time waiting) versus 162.7 minutes (44% of agent time waiting). [3] This aligns with our feeling that locally running agents are often "doing nothing" while waiting on test results, each other, and so on

- The possibility to monitor "input channels" (e.g. chat channels, e-mail inboxes...) and have agents act autonomously on those seems like something that could help us out as well.

This all sounds amazing, but we're unsure how others are currently doing this and what those cost. We currently mainly power our needs via subscription-based contracts (e.g. claude (code) pro/max, chatgpt plus/pro ...)

- Is anyone running such multi-agent or always-on agent systems?

- Do you host it yourself, or do you use existings solutions like grok bots or claude remote control sessions or claude routines?

- Can you make this work with subscriptions, or do you use API pricing, or even self-hosted LLMs? How do the costs compare with running local agents?

- How are the results? Is it an improvement?

[1] Stanford CS146S: How always-on agents work

Lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1OBRtfPS34

Slides: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1b8WiBk_lcB3ue-jZMLijSUMLj6SDiF6Z/view

[2] CMU 11-768 AI Agents: https://www.cmu-agents.com/#/schedule

[3] Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Shared Context (figure 3, page 3): https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.10662

title.value: Ask HN: Is anyone running multi/always-on agents that don't cost a fortune?
